Where it began

Bob Woolmer was born on 14 May 1948 in Kanpur, India, in a hospital just over the road from the Green Park ground. Cricket was in the family: his father, Clarence Woolmer, played Ranji Trophy cricket for United Provinces. As a boy of ten he watched Hanif Mohammad make 499 in Karachi.

He went to school in Kent, first in Tonbridge and then at The Skinners' School, and at 15 was turned from an off-spinner into a medium-pace bowler. He joined the Kent staff in 1968, won his county cap the next year and gained his coaching qualification early, at the same time as his playing career began.

The player

He came into the England side in 1975 as an all-rounder, on the strength of a hat-trick for MCC against Australia's visiting side. At The Oval that summer he made 149 batting at number five. It was not a quick innings, but it was a long and valuable one, and two more hundreds against Australia followed in 1977. All three of his Test centuries came against the Australians.

In all he played 19 Tests between 1975 and 1981, scoring 1,059 runs at 33.09. In 1978 he helped Kent to a double of the Championship and the Benson and Hedges Cup, and was man of the match in the cup final.

What made him special

His real gift was for teaching. He ran his own cricket school as a young man and later coached in South Africa, at schools and at the Avendale club in Cape Town, where his influence led to a yearly programme sending a young player to England for a summer. At Warwickshire he oversaw a run of trophies in the mid-1990s, and he was on hand when Brian Lara made 501 not out in 1994. He may well be the only person who saw both that innings and Hanif's 499.

As coach of South Africa he won the ICC KnockOut Trophy in 1998, the country's first ICC title. He was an early champion of computer analysis, helped make the reverse sweep a popular shot and borrowed ideas from football goalkeepers to help wicketkeepers. Later, with Pakistan, he led the side to a drawn Test series and an ODI series win in India in 2005.

Away from the middle

Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 1976. Pakistan honoured him with the Sitara-e-Imtiaz for his work with their cricket, and the national indoor academy in Lahore bears his name. He died in 2007.

And finally

In Kanpur the Green Park ground, beside the hospital where he was born, has the nickname Woolmer's Turf, and the street around it is Woolmer Street. Not many coaches have a road named after them in the town they left as a child.
